Don't build a wrapper around the data — build one around Polars expressions. Expressions are plain Python objects, so you can generate them programmatically and never hand-write `c1*c48 + c2*c49 + ...`:

```python
import polars as pl

def matvec(M, v, prefix="y"):
    """M: list of rows of column names, v: tuple of vector column names."""
    return [
        sum(pl.col(a) * pl.col(b) for a, b in zip(row, v)).alias(f"{prefix}_{i}")
        for i, row in enumerate(M)
    ]

q = (
    pl.scan_parquet("events.parquet")
    .with_columns(matvec(
        [("c1", "c2", "c3"), ("c4", "c5", "c6"), ("c7", "c8", "c9")],
        ("c48", "c49", "c50"),
    ))
)
df = q.collect(engine="streaming")
```

Chaining is just calling it again: a second `.with_columns(matvec(...))` that references the generated `y_*` names stays inside the same lazy plan, so the streaming engine still batches everything and never loads the full dataset. Matrix–matrix products are simply N matvecs (one per output column), so the same helper covers them.

Keep everything in expression form — `map_batches` with NumPy would pull data out of the streaming engine and reintroduce manual batching.

The BashOperator doesn't push your Python variable to XCom — it pushes **the last line written to stdout by the whole bash command**. If `myscript.py` only `logging.info(...)`s the value (logging goes to stderr) or assigns it to a variable, stdout is empty, so the XCom shows nothing.

Fix: make the script print the value as the final line of stdout:

```python
# myscript.py
# ... logging uses stderr, that's fine ...
print(file_path)   # last stdout line -> pushed to XCom
```

Ensure nothing else prints to stdout after that line (redirect other output to stderr or a log file). `do_xcom_push=True` is already the default in Airflow 2.

Then pull it in the second command with the Jinja template, e.g.:

```python
bash_command=(
    f"python secondscript.py --dag_id '{dag.dag_id}' "
    f"--task_id '{second_task_id}' "
    f"--file '{{{{ ti.xcom_pull(task_ids='{first_task_id}') }}}}'"
)
```

Note the `{{{{ }}}}` escaping needed because it's inside an f-string; your current escaped-quote version may also render incorrectly. Verify via UI → first task → XCom that the value appears before testing the pull.

**Likely cause:** `.gcno` files are emitted by the compiler next to each `.o`, but Bazel only keeps files it knows about as declared action outputs. Native C++ compile actions run with `--collect_code_coverage` declare the `.gcno` and copy it into `bazel-out/`; your custom python-scripted targets do not, so their `.gcno` files are created inside the action sandbox and silently discarded when the action finishes. That's why only the files compiled through real `cc_*` rules have them.

You can confirm this by building with `--spawn_strategy=standalone` (or `--sandbox_debug` and inspecting the sandbox dir) — you'll see the "missing" `.gcno` files appear in the execroot.

**Fix:** declare the `.gcno` as an output of your custom action so Bazel preserves it:

```python
obj = ctx.actions.declare_file(ctx.label.name + ".o")
gcno = ctx.actions.declare_file(ctx.label.name + ".gcno", sibling = obj)
ctx.actions.run(
    outputs = [obj, gcno],
    executable = ctx.executable._wrapper,
    arguments = [...],  # must place gcno at gcno.path
)
```

Alternatively, build those sources with `cc_library` and add them to `--instrumentation_filter`, letting Bazel handle gcno/gcda collection natively.

**Cause:** `ExpectColumnValuesToBeIncreasing` relies on the `column_values.increasing` metric, which computes `column.diff().ge(0)`. For a `datetime64` column, `diff()` returns `Timedelta` values, and pandas raises `TypeError` when comparing `Timedelta >= 0` (an int). So the expectation simply doesn’t support datetime dtypes in this GX/pandas version combination — it works fine for numeric columns.

**Fix / workaround:** validate an integer representation of the timestamp instead of the datetime itself:

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("Test Calendar.csv", parse_dates=["Date"])
# seconds since epoch (monotonic with time)
df["Date_num"] = df["Date"].astype("int64") // 10**9

suite.add_expectation(
    gx.expectations.ExpectColumnValuesToBeIncreasing(column="Date_num")
)
```

Then validate as before. `strictly=True/False` behaves normally on the numeric column.

Also check for a newer Great Expectations release — datetime support in this metric has been an open issue, and upgrading may fix it natively. The text of your question doesn’t include your GX/pandas versions, so I can’t confirm which patch applies.

**Cause:** `proc.standardOutput` is not a valid property of the Process object returned by `system()` in TeXstudio macros, so `output` is `undefined` — that's why `alert(output)` is empty and nothing gets inserted. What you see in the Messages panel is just the raw stdout of the external command echoed by TeXstudio. You must read the output with `readAllStandardOutput()`.

**Fix (macro):**

```javascript
%SCRIPT
var proc = system("/home/stefan/ARCHIVE/SCRIPTS/latex_automation/main.py");
proc.waitForFinished();
var output = proc.readAllStandardOutput().replace(/\s+$/, "");
editor.insertText(output);
```

Also check:

1. The macro must start with `%SCRIPT` on the first line, otherwise `insertText`/JS is not executed as script code.
2. Remove `repr()` in the Python script — it wraps the string in quotes that would end up in your `.tex` file:

```python
print(str(fn) + "xxxx", end="")
```

3. `proc.readAllStandardError()` is available for debugging if the script misbehaves.

With these changes the string returned by Python is inserted at the cursor position of the current `.tex` document.

This is almost certainly SELinux on Fedora blocking the memory mapping (`mmap` with `PROT_EXEC`) of numpy's compiled `.so` files — the classic cause of `failed to map segment from shared object` under mod_wsgi. Rocky 9 differs because of different policy/boolean state there.

Confirm by checking for AVC denials:

    sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent | grep httpd

Fix by enabling the boolean that allows httpd to map executable memory:

    sudo setsebool -P httpd_execmem 1

then restart Apache:

    sudo systemctl restart httpd

Two related things to verify if that doesn't clear it:

1. The venv lives under `/var/www/html`, which is labeled `httpd_sys_content_t` (non-executable). Move the venv somewhere like `/opt/test/venv` or relabel with `httpd_sys_script_exec_t`, and update `sys.path.insert`.
2. Ensure `/var/www` isn't mounted `noexec` (`mount | grep /var`).

As a quick diagnostic, `sudo setenforce 0` — if the import then succeeds, SELinux is definitively the cause, and you can re-enable enforcing after applying the boolean.

This error comes from a mismatch between `unsloth 2024.8` and `transformers 4.44.2`. In 4.44 the KV-cache API changed again, so the cache object Unsloth/PEFT creates during training or generation never gets populated, and the first `cache.update(...)`/`layer_idx` access fails with "0 layers".

Unsloth 2024.8 is validated against the 4.43.x line, so the fix is to pin transformers to the latest 4.43 release instead of 4.44.2:

```bash
pip install transformers==4.43.3
```

Since you only need `>= 4.43.0` for the Unsloth dependency, 4.43.3 satisfies that requirement and stays within Unsloth's supported range.

If you still see the error after pinning, disable caching during training, since `use_cache=True` is incompatible with gradient checkpointing and can trigger the empty-cache path:

```python
model.config.use_cache = False
# re-enable only for inference:
outputs = model.generate(..., use_cache=True)
```

Keep `torch 2.3.0` and `unsloth 2024.8` as they are; only the transformers pin should change.

**This is not a Python 3.14 / pywin32 issue.** If pywin32 didn't support your interpreter you'd get an `ImportError`, not "Server execution failed". That error (`CO_E_SERVER_EXEC_FAILURE`, 0x80080005) means COM tried to *launch* OUTLOOK.EXE as a local server and the launch failed.

**Most likely cause: New Outlook.** The new Outlook client does not implement the classic `Outlook.Application` COM server, and switching to it breaks/redirects the registration even if classic Outlook files remain on disk. Fix:

1. Open classic Outlook and turn off the "New Outlook" toggle, or set classic Outlook as the default mail app (Settings → Apps → Default apps).
2. If classic Outlook was removed by the switch, reinstall it or run an **Online Repair** of Office, which re-registers the COM server.

Verify outside Python first:

```
powershell -c "New-Object -ComObject Outlook.Application"
```

If that succeeds, `win32com.client.Dispatch("Outlook.Application")` will work.

Secondary cause to rule out: elevation mismatch — if your script runs elevated but Outlook doesn't (or vice versa), COM activation fails. Run both at the same integrity level.

Two likely causes:

**1. Package name mismatch.** Your project is `dojipipeline` but the package directory is `mypackage`. uv's default build backend (hatchling) looks for a package matching the project name, so `src/mypackage` (and its `j2/` folder) never gets packaged. Fix it explicitly:

```toml
[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]
packages = ["src/mypackage"]
```

(or rename the directory to `src/dojipipeline`).

**2. Ignored files.** Hatchling includes non-`.py` files inside the package by default, but excludes anything matched by `.gitignore`. If your templates are ignored, force them in:

```toml
[tool.hatch.build]
artifacts = ["*.j2"]
```

Then load templates relative to the installed package, not the working directory:

```python
from jinja2 import Environment, PackageLoader

env = Environment(loader=PackageLoader("mypackage", "j2"))
tpl = env.get_template("generate_data_model.j2")
```

Verify with `uv build` and inspect the wheel (`unzip -l dist/*.whl`) — you should see `mypackage/j2/*.j2` entries. After that you can drop the docstring workaround entirely.

Use NumPy slicing. If `M` is a 4×4 `np.array`, the 2×2 blocks are just sub-ranges of rows and columns:

```python
import numpy as np

M = np.array([[A11, A12, A13, A14],
              [A21, A22, A23, A24],
              [A31, A32, A33, A34],
              [A41, A42, A43, A44]])

A = M[:2, :2]   # rows 0-1, cols 0-1
B = M[:2, 2:]   # rows 0-1, cols 2-3
C = M[2:, :2]   # rows 2-3, cols 0-1
D = M[2:, 2:]   # rows 2-3, cols 2-3
```

These are **views**, not copies — modifying `A` also modifies `M`. Use `M[:2, :2].copy()` if you need independent arrays.

For unequal block sizes, slice at arbitrary indices, e.g. `M[:3, :3]`, `M[:3, 3:]`, `M[3:, :3]`, `M[3:, 3:]`.

To go the other way (rebuild `M` from blocks), use `np.block`:

```python
M = np.block([[A, B], [C, D]])
```

You can also automate splitting of an `n×n` matrix into `k×k` blocks with `np.split(M, k, axis=0/1)` or by reshaping: `M.reshape(2, 2, 2, 2).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)`.

`mad()` was deprecated in pandas 1.5 and **removed in pandas 2.0**, so it no longer exists in 2.1.4. There is no single replacement method; compute it manually instead.

The old behavior (mean absolute deviation from the mean) is reproduced with:

```python
# Series
s.sub(s.mean()).abs().mean()

# DataFrame (column-wise, same as the old df.mad())
df.sub(df.mean(axis=0)).abs().mean(axis=0)

# or equivalently with NumPy
import numpy as np
np.abs(df - df.mean()).mean()
```

Example:

```python
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4])
s.sub(s.mean()).abs().mean()   # 1.0, same as s.mad() in older versions
```

Notes:

- `mean()` skips `NaN` by default (`skipna=True`), matching the old `mad()` behavior. Use `df.mean(..., skipna=False)` if you need NaN propagation.
- Don't confuse this with the *median* absolute deviation — if that's what you want, use `scipy.stats.median_abs_deviation(s)`.

The 403 isn't a User-Agent problem. NYSCEF's `ViewDocument` endpoint validates server-side session state: the `docIndex` token is only honored after your session has loaded the case's document list and accepted the terms of use. Additionally, the site sits behind a WAF that rejects `requests`' non-browser TLS fingerprint, so even copied cookies often still return 403.

Fix: establish the session in the browser first, then let Chrome download the PDF:

```python
import os
from seleniumbase import SB

dl = os.path.abspath("downloads")
with SB(headless=False) as sb:  # old headless mode is more likely to be blocked
    sb.driver.execute_cdp_cmd(
        "Page.setDownloadBehavior",
        {"behavior": "allow", "downloadPath": dl})
    sb.open("https://iapps.courts.state.ny.us/nyscef/CaseSearch?...")  # load case, accept terms
    sb.open(doc_url)  # only now request the document
    sb.sleep(8)
```

With downloads enabled there is no `<embed>` — the file lands in `downloads/`. If you must use `requests`, transfer `sb.get_cookies()` and use `curl_cffi` (`requests.get(url, impersonate="chrome", cookies=...)`) to mimic Chrome's TLS handshake.

Finally, verify the document is actually public — sealed/restricted filings return 403 even in a real browser.

Yes — it's allowed, because in Tk every widget *is* a window, and any window can contain other windows. Tkinter does no special validation of `master`: a `Label`, `Button`, even an `Entry` will happily accept children, and they'll be stacked and managed by the geometry manager like anywhere else.

However, it's strongly discouraged:

1. **Portability**: widgets are rendered differently per platform (and per theme). A `Button` on Windows is often drawn by the OS, and children placed inside it may not appear, may flicker, or may be overdrawn. The fact that it "works" on your Linux box is an accident of how that platform draws buttons, not a guarantee.
2. **Semantics**: clicking the button, tab traversal, and focus events become ambiguous when it contains an interactive child like `Entry`.
3. **Maintainability**: future Tk versions or themes can change how a widget paints itself, breaking your layout.

The correct pattern is to wrap things in a container:

```python
wrapper = tk.Frame(master=frame)
wrapper.pack(side=tk.TOP)

entry1 = tk.Entry(master=wrapper, bg="#fff", fg="#000")
entry1.pack()
```

Rule of thumb: parent only to `Tk`, `Frame` (or `ttk.Frame`), `Toplevel`, `Canvas`, and `LabelFrame`/`PanedWindow`. Use `Frame` when you want to group widgets — that's exactly what it's for.

No — this isn't possible. PEP 646, which introduced `TypeVarTuple`, deliberately supports only a small set of operations: using `*Ts` as-is (`tuple[*Ts]`), concatenating (`tuple[*Ts, int]`, `tuple[int, *Ts]`), and unpacking into other variadic generics. There is no "map" operation that applies a type constructor like `list` element-wise, so `tuple[list[T] for T in *Ts]` has no valid syntax, and `list[*Ts]` is also rejected because `list` takes exactly one type parameter.

The standard workaround is a set of `@overload`s enumerating the arities you care about:

```python
from typing import overload, TypeVar

T1, T2 = TypeVar("T1"), TypeVar("T2")

@overload
def foo(t: tuple[()]) -> tuple[()]: ...
@overload
def foo(t: tuple[T1]) -> tuple[list[T1]]: ...
@overload
def foo(t: tuple[T1, T2]) -> tuple[list[T1], list[T2]]: ...

def foo(t):
    return tuple([x] for x in t)  # implementation
```

"Mapping" over variadic tuples has been proposed in typing discussions (see PEP 646's "Transforming TypeVarTuples" section), but nothing has been accepted, so as of current Python it remains unsupported.

**Cause:** `Q` is a reserved name in SymPy — it's the `ask.Q` assumptions object (`sympy.assumptions.ask.Q`). When you pass the *string* `'Q'` to `solve`, SymPy parses it via `sympify`/`parse_expr`, which resolves names against SymPy's own namespace first. So `'Q'` becomes the `AssumptionKeys` object instead of `Symbol('Q')`, and the internal substitution then fails with `SympifyError`. Lowercase `'q'` isn't a SymPy name, so it parses cleanly as a symbol. The same collision happens with `'I'`, `'E'`, `'S'`, `'N'`, `'O'`, `'pi'`, `'beta'`, etc.

**Fix:** pass actual Symbol objects, or create `Q` as a symbol with `symbols`:

```python
from sympy import *

x, y, Q = symbols('x y Q')
gf = x + y, 5*x - y - Q
k = solve(gf, x, y, dict=True)
```

Note two other issues in your snippet: `Q = 1` made `Q` the integer 1 (so it vanished from the equations), and passing multiple symbols as separate positional arguments is fragile — use a list/tuple like `solve(gf, (x, y, Q))`.

You didn't post the actual error, but there are two usual culprits here.

**1) `common` isn't importable from user-service's venv.** Declare it as a Poetry path dependency in `user-service/pyproject.toml`:

```toml
[tool.poetry.dependencies]
common = { path = "../common", develop = true }
```

then `poetry install`. Make sure `common/__init__.py` and `common/tests/__init__.py` exist so `common.tests.db_conf` resolves as a module.

**2) `pytest_plugins` is only honored in the *root* conftest.py.** In a non-root conftest it emits a deprecation warning on pytest 7.2+ and an error on pytest 8. Move it up:

```python
# user-service/conftest.py
pytest_plugins = ["common.tests.db_conf"]
```

Note you don't need both mechanisms: your direct `from common.tests.db_conf import ...` already registers those fixtures, since pytest collects any `@pytest.fixture` object present in the conftest namespace. Also drop `pytest_plugins = ["anyio"]` from `db_conf.py` — it's ignored in plugin modules, and anyio's plugin is auto-loaded via its `pytest11` entry point anyway.

Your post only includes Issue 1 (the body cuts off before the expected result and Issues 2–3), but here's what's happening with the text:

`style.element_options('Button.label')` lists options the label element *can render*, but that doesn't mean you can set them via `style.configure`. For options like `text`, `image`, and `compound`, ttk.Button's implementation feeds the element the widget's own option values every time it redraws, so the widget always overrides the style database. `style.configure('TButton', text='my button')` does store a `text` entry in the style (which is why it shows up when you query the style back), but it's shadowed at draw time by the button's own `text` option, which defaults to `''`.

Styles are meant to control *appearance* (background, font, padding, relief); label content is per-widget state:

```python
b = ttk.Button(root, text='my button')
# or later:
b.configure(text='my button')
```

So this isn't a bug — it's how ttk separates widget data from theming. If you edit in Issues 2 and 3, they can be addressed as well.
